title: What the Town Next Door Adds to a Cancer Map — Besag Spatial Markov Fields, Clayton–Kaldor Empirical Bayes Shrinkage & Besag–York–Mollié (BYM) Spatial Smoothing of Male Lip & Laryngeal Cancer Maps

teenKit.tldr: In 15 seconds: On raw county cancer maps, tiny rural counties always dominate both the 'highest risk' and 'lowest risk' extremes just by small-number coin flips. Besag–York–Mollie (BYM) spatial smoothing borrows information from neighboring towns to reveal real environmental gradients.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Sending public-health teams after small-denominator noise misses true regional cancer hazards in larger or neighboring communities.
keyTakeaways: Standardized Mortality/Incidence Ratios (O_i / E_i) have huge variance when expected counts E_i are small (e.g., E_i = 1.5 cases).

Clayton & Kaldor (1987) shrank noisy ratios toward a global mean, and Besag, York & Mollie (1991) split log relative risk into spatially structured neighbor smoothing (ICAR) plus unstructured local noise.
In Scottish lip cancer maps, spatial borrowing stabilizes tiny-county outliers and reveals a clear coastal/outdoor solar-exposure gradient.

vocab.meaning: Observed cases divided by age-standardized expected cases in region i.
Intrinsic Conditional Autoregressive prior where each region's spatial effect centers on the average of its bordering neighbors.
Besag–York–Mollie convolution combining spatially correlated neighbor effects with independent area-level heterogeneity.

quiz.question: Why do sparsely populated counties disproportionately appear at both the top and bottom of raw cancer rate rankings?
options: Rural air both causes and cures cancer simultaneously
Poisson sampling variance of O_i / E_i scales inversely with expected count E_i, so tiny denominators swing wildly on 1 or 2 extra cases
quiz.explanation: When E_i is tiny, Var(O_i / E_i) = theta / E_i is huge, making extreme high and low raw ratios mostly small-sample noise.
